title: A life across the boundary
introduction: These are illustrated, fictional scenarios, not interviews. Thoughts and scenes are imagined; source-linked facts appear when we zoom out. Characters can overlap and do not represent measured population shares.
cityThesis: More movement can connect two cities, but stronger livelihoods, relationships and participation must be checked separately.
cityThesisStatus: Analytical proposition to investigate, not a measured citywide effect.
presentationRules: Keep the selected character visible from their three story beats through all four city lenses.
Display the fiction label with first-person bubbles. Bubbles and personal passages are scenarios, never interview quotations.
The city passage is the factual zoom-out. Attach its source links and retain each caveat in the evidence view.
Directions describe only the named measure, arrangement or evidence gap. They are not resilience scores or quantified character outcomes.
Keep the student a student. Do not use nursing vacancies or adult employment figures as their lived experience.
Show questions as questions. Do not draw a positive or negative trend for an unmeasured connection or participation outcome.
Equal-sized characters and schematic links do not encode prevalence, population share, trip volume or effect size.

Sequence: human stories, aggregate city picture, four dimensions and their evidence, specific frictions and responses, then Singapore–Johor. Future five-year-plan examples belong in the later responses chapter.

characters.title: The weekend user
characters.configuration: Lives and works in Hong Kong; visits Shenzhen for leisure.

storyBeats.label: A Saturday in Sheung Shui
storyBeats.bubble: Lunch here, or take the train north?
storyBeats.context: At the footbridge between Sheung Shui Centre and the station, local shops and a northbound journey sit side by side.

storyBeats.label: Before I pay
storyBeats.bubble: Which shops do I want to keep coming back to?
storyBeats.context: At a café counter, choice becomes a question about where everyday spending lands.

storyBeats.label: Home for the evening
storyBeats.bubble: I’m back. Shall we meet downstairs?
storyBeats.context: Back in Hong Kong, familiar neighbours are still part of this imagined evening.

lenses.bubble: My lunch money crosses the border. What does that mean for local shops?
lenses.personal: This day out places one purchase in Shenzhen while home and work remain in Hong Kong.
lenses.city: Hong Kong retail company counts fell 3.9% in 2023–24; Shenzhen’s Hong Kong–Macao overnight visitor-trips rose 26.6% in 2025. Different measures and periods do not establish a spending transfer.
lenses.lesson: Ask who benefits and who adjusts. A visitor increase and a company-count decline cannot show where one shopper’s money went.
lenses.direction: Separate economic signals; no measured transfer
lenses.caveat: Retail counts are not closures or fixed firms. The visitor series combines Hong Kong and Macao, excludes day visitors and does not measure this fictional day trip.

lenses.bubble: I enjoyed the trip. My familiar faces are still waiting at home.
lenses.personal: The imagined return home keeps established relationships in view even when a purchase happens elsewhere.
lenses.city: Do leisure visits change attachment to either city? The reviewed evidence does not establish a citywide direction for weekend visitors.
lenses.lesson: Follow recurring relationships as well as purchases. Spending across a boundary does not by itself demonstrate weaker belonging.

lenses.bubble: Getting across is one thing. Can I count on the journey home?
lenses.personal: A day out needs an outward route and a return. This scenario makes reliability a question, not an assumed benefit.
lenses.city: Hong Kong-resident departures through seven direct Shenzhen boundary points rose from 75.3 million in 2024 to 85.8 million in 2025. They count movements, not people or trip purposes.
lenses.lesson: More crossings show greater use. Check waiting, reliability and accessibility separately before calling the system more resilient.
lenses.caveat: Analyst sums of rounded control-point counts. Final destinations are unknown; West Kowloon high-speed rail and the Hong Kong–Zhuhai–Macao Bridge are excluded.

lenses.bubble: Where would I make time to help out?
lenses.personal: After the outing, a neighbourhood invitation raises a different choice: where to give time, attention or help.
lenses.city: Do weekend visitors join local events, volunteer or offer community feedback differently? The reviewed sources do not establish a direction in either city.
lenses.lesson: Measure time and contribution directly. Shopping frequency cannot stand in for community participation.

characters.title: The northbound relocator
characters.configuration: Moves home from Hong Kong to Shenzhen while retaining Hong Kong ties.

storyBeats.label: A different front door
storyBeats.bubble: I’ve moved in. I’ll call my friends in Hong Kong tonight.
storyBeats.context: A bag arrives at an imagined Shenzhen home; familiar ties remain across the boundary.

storyBeats.label: The practical list
storyBeats.bubble: Groceries are sorted. Where would I go for follow-up care?
storyBeats.context: Unpacking opens a second list: services, appointments and the rules that apply to them.

storyBeats.label: The next hello
storyBeats.bubble: Maybe I’ll stop and chat instead of walking straight upstairs.
storyBeats.context: The relocator pauses beside a neighbour, opening a small possibility for local connection.

lenses.bubble: My address has moved. Which parts of my week will follow?
lenses.personal: Moving home leaves this character deciding which routines to build in Shenzhen and which connections to keep in Hong Kong.
lenses.city: In 2017, schooling and work made up 45.4% and 19.8% of trips by Hong Kong residents living in the Mainland. These historical trip purposes do not measure present livelihoods.
lenses.lesson: Map home, work and learning separately. A residential move need not put every part of a life in the same city.
lenses.direction: Historical work and school links documented
lenses.caveat: Trips by the stated resident group, not shares of all relocators or unique people. Do not treat 2017 purpose shares as current.

lenses.bubble: I know the way home. When will this street feel familiar?
lenses.personal: A new address creates the setting for repeated encounters; this fictional greeting does not guarantee friendship or belonging.
lenses.city: When does residence become a network of local relationships? The reviewed material does not establish a citywide connection trend among northbound relocators.
lenses.lesson: Ask about recurring contacts and mutual support. An address or a nearby border cannot measure social connection.

lenses.bubble: Can my care move with my home?
lenses.personal: In this scenario, moving home raises another question: which services can follow me, and on what terms?
lenses.city: The 2026/27 HA pilot subsidises designated follow-up at HKU–Shenzhen Hospital for eligible patients, with a RMB2,000 annual cap; inpatient and A&E care are excluded.
lenses.lesson: A route between cities is only one layer of access. Eligibility, matching clinics and continuity rules also matter.
lenses.direction: A defined care route with eligibility conditions
lenses.caveat: No eligibility is asserted for the fictional character. This pilot is not the elderly voucher scheme. First subsidised service normally cancels the corresponding HA follow-up; specified exceptions and return referral apply.

lenses.bubble: I live here now. How could I take part?
lenses.personal: A neighbourhood notice becomes an invitation to ask where this new resident could contribute or raise an everyday concern.
lenses.city: Are cross-border residents joining activities, offering mutual help or giving local feedback in Shenzhen? The reviewed evidence does not establish their participation or its direction.
lenses.lesson: Distinguish available opportunities from actual involvement. A community space does not tell us who uses it or feels heard.

characters.title: The cross-border student
characters.configuration: Lives in Shenzhen and attends school in Hong Kong.

storyBeats.label: Before the school bell
storyBeats.bubble: School starts across the boundary. I’ve packed my homework.
storyBeats.context: The fictional student leaves home in Shenzhen with a schoolbag and a route to a Hong Kong classroom.

storyBeats.label: At the classroom door
storyBeats.bubble: I know the route. Do I feel part of the class?
storyBeats.context: Arriving at school opens a question about peers and belonging, beyond simply reaching the building.

storyBeats.label: An after-school invitation
storyBeats.bubble: I’d like to join the club. How would getting home work?
storyBeats.context: A classmate’s invitation brings school participation and the journey home into the same imagined decision.

lenses.bubble: My classroom is in Hong Kong. What does that make possible?
lenses.personal: Learning connects this student to Hong Kong; it does not make them a worker or establish a future wage.
lenses.city: The September 2024 school survey counted 16,139 cross-boundary students across kindergarten, primary and secondary schools. It measures enrolment, not attainment, household costs or future earnings.
lenses.lesson: For this character, begin with access to learning. Keep student evidence separate from adult labour and shortage statistics.

lenses.bubble: Who will I sit with today?
lenses.personal: A familiar classmate makes connection visible in this imagined school day. The bubble is not a pupil’s recorded testimony.
lenses.city: In an observational study of 417 cross-border pupils, peer relationships were associated with belonging. The finding concerns that sample, not either city as a whole.
lenses.lesson: Look beyond arrival at school to relationships within it. An association is a useful clue, not proof of what causes belonging.
lenses.direction: Peer relationships linked with belonging in one sample
lenses.caveat: No effect size or citywide direction is established here. The study does not describe every cross-border student.

lenses.bubble: There’s a route to school. How does a school place get decided?
lenses.personal: This student’s journey introduces a wider family question: transport and access to a school place are separate practical matters.
lenses.city: For 2027 P1 admission, eligible cross-boundary applicants retain unrestricted discretionary and Part A choices; Part B uses a dedicated list generally near boundary points.
lenses.lesson: Put service rules beside transport links. Keep a family’s school-choice options visible rather than drawing the border as the only gate.
lenses.direction: School access follows distinct allocation routes
lenses.caveat: A P1 policy example, not a claim that this depicted student is currently applying. One discretionary school and up to three Part A choices; POA covers government and aided schools.

lenses.bubble: Could I stay and join in?
lenses.personal: The imagined club invitation turns participation into an everyday choice about school life and getting home.
lenses.city: In the 417-pupil observational study, extracurricular participation was associated with belonging. This school-level finding does not establish citywide volunteering, civic participation or a causal effect.
lenses.lesson: Ask what makes joining in possible. School activities provide a bounded clue; wider community contribution needs its own evidence.
lenses.direction: Extracurricular participation linked with belonging in one sample
lenses.caveat: Commuting hours were not statistically significant in that sample. This does not prove that journeys have no effect or that every student can attend activities.

characters.title: The southbound newcomer
characters.configuration: Moves from the Mainland to Hong Kong for work in this fictional scenario, retaining Mainland ties.

storyBeats.label: A new route home
storyBeats.bubble: New room, new route. I’ll learn the neighbourhood one walk at a time.
storyBeats.context: The imagined newcomer walks home in Hong Kong; their prior Mainland city is deliberately unspecified.

storyBeats.label: After the working day
storyBeats.bubble: I know where I work. Where do I go after work?
storyBeats.context: The route between home and work is taking shape, while social routines remain an open question.

storyBeats.label: An invitation nearby
storyBeats.bubble: Could I come along next time?
storyBeats.context: An invitation to a neighbourhood activity makes a possible connection visible, without assuming it becomes lasting.

lenses.bubble: Starting work is one step. What will help me build a life here?
lenses.personal: In this fictional work-led move, finding a routine extends beyond the workplace. No visa route or employment outcome is assigned.
lenses.city: Hong Kong approved 26,714 new ASMTP applications in 2025. Approvals record one admission route; they do not count settled newcomers, identify Shenzhen origins or show employment outcomes.
lenses.lesson: Separate permission to enter from settlement and a sustainable livelihood. Neither an approval nor this story measures successful integration.
lenses.direction: Admission approvals documented; settlement outcomes unknown

lenses.bubble: Who will become a familiar face outside work?
lenses.personal: The imagined newcomer looks for people and places to return to, while retaining relationships elsewhere.
lenses.city: How do newcomers build recurring relationships in Hong Kong, and what role does Shenzhen proximity play? The reviewed evidence does not establish a citywide direction.
lenses.lesson: Ask where relationships actually form. A move, a job and a nearby border do not by themselves measure belonging.
lenses.direction: Newcomer connection remains an open question

lenses.bubble: Can I reach the people and places that matter to me?
lenses.personal: The imagined newcomer learns a route to work while thinking about the relationships and services they want to keep within reach.
lenses.city: How do daily routes and cross-border ties fit together after a move? The reviewed evidence does not establish newcomers’ journey reliability or access across Hong Kong.
lenses.lesson: Check the journeys people actually need. Aggregate crossing counts cannot tell us whether a newcomer can reach work, services and relationships reliably.

lenses.bubble: Is there a place where I could join in and be heard?
lenses.personal: A local invitation offers this character a possible first step; the story leaves room for practical barriers and different choices.
lenses.city: Do newcomers gain opportunities to contribute, volunteer and give neighbourhood feedback? The reviewed sources do not establish their participation or its direction across Hong Kong.
lenses.lesson: Track invitations, access and repeated involvement separately. Moving in or working locally does not tell us whether someone feels able to contribute.

responseExamples.bubble: Which connections can I use now, and which are still plans?
responseExamples.personal: A new home makes transport plans feel personal, but a line on a future map cannot determine this newcomer’s actual journey.
responseExamples.city: Hong Kong’s 2026–2030 plan aims for the Northern Link Main and Spur lines in 2034 and the Hong Kong–Shenzhen Western Rail Link in 2035. These are future commissioning aims.
responseExamples.lesson: Keep today’s routes separate from future plans, then test who can actually reach work, services and people.
responseExamples.direction: Future connectivity planned; outcomes not yet observed
responseExamples.caveat: Targets are not completed routes or guaranteed opening dates. Do not assume the character lives near these projects or originated in Shenzhen.
responseExamples.label: A planned response, not a route open today
